findings.title: Async legacy write derives from request context and gets canceled
findings.body: Each background goroutine wraps the request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. The request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy write will therefore often be canceled before or while it runs. The context also carries request-scoped values whose lifetime ends with the request. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the base, then apply the timeout. The same pattern appears at lines 110, 135 and 163.

findings.title: Legacy write errors are silently dropped
findings.body: Errors from the async Legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls only feed the duration metric. They are never logged. Legacy store divergence will go unnoticed and be hard to debug. Log the error, using the `log` logger, inside each goroutine.

findings.title: Storage failure recorded as legacy duration
findings.body: When the Storage Create call fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy store in metrics. Update has the same mistake at line 129.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration
findings.body: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy timings end up in the storage metric and skew it.

findings.title: Delete metric uses name as kind label
findings.body: In Delete, the success path passes `name` where `options.Kind` is expected. Every object name becomes its own value of the kind label, which creates unbounded metric cardinality. Separately, line 97 calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of passing `log`, so the logger stored in the context loses the name, kind and method fields.

findings.title: Legacy update re-applies objInfo against a different base
findings.body: The async legacy Update reuses the original `objInfo` instead of wrapping the object that unified storage returned. The previous code used `updateWrapper` for this. Patch-style updates will be recomputed against the legacy object, which can produce divergent data between the two stores.

findings.title: Tests are racy and don't verify async legacy calls
findings.body: The goroutines may call the shared mock after the test returns, and nothing asserts that the legacy methods were actually invoked. In the Create error case, the setup function registers the failing expectation on the legacy mock rather than on storage. That case only passes because the shared mock answers storage calls too.
